_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 590 words, six questions in text order). Test 2 leans on attitude and inference: most questions ask what the writer feels, suggests or realises rather than what happened. Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 2.
title: Out of my depth
subtitle: Journalist Clare Moss was forty-three when she finally decided to learn to swim. She describes a year in the shallow end.

cards.text: For most of my life I had a well-practised routine for avoiding water. On beach holidays I volunteered to look after the bags. At friends' pool parties I arrived late, with a story about a cold I was just getting over. Nobody ever questioned it, and I came to believe that nobody had noticed. It was my nine-year-old nephew who finally said, quite kindly, what everyone else had apparently known for years: 'Auntie Clare, you can't swim, can you?' I laughed, and told him of course I could. Then I went home and looked up adult lessons at the local pool.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about her nephew's question?
choices: It showed her that her secret had never really been a secret.
It was the first time anyone had invited her to swim.
It upset her because he asked it in front of other people.
It reminded her of an embarrassing beach holiday.
cards.highlight: what everyone else had apparently known for years
cards.why: 'What everyone else had apparently known for years': she had believed nobody noticed, and he proved they had. Nothing says others were present, so C has no support.

cards.text: The class met on Tuesday evenings, and there were six of us. I had expected to be the oldest by some distance, but the others ranged from a student of twenty to a retired bus driver called Leonard, who was seventy-one. What we had in common, it turned out, was not age but a particular kind of fear. None of us was afraid of drowning, exactly. We were afraid of looking foolish. Our instructor, Bea, understood this immediately. On the first evening she did not ask us to get into the water at all. She simply sat with us on the edge and talked.
cards.question: What did the writer discover about the other people in the class?
choices: Most of them were much younger than she was.
They had all had a frightening experience in water.
They shared her worry about how they would appear to others.
They were less nervous than she had expected.
cards.highlight: We were afraid of looking foolish.
cards.why: The shared fear is 'not age' and not drowning but 'looking foolish'. A is wrong because Leonard is seventy-one; B confuses fear of water with fear of embarrassment.

cards.text: Bea's method was slow, and at first I found it maddening. For three weeks we did little more than stand in the shallow end and put our faces in the water, counting to five. I had paid for swimming lessons, I told my husband, not breathing lessons. He pointed out, reasonably, that I had never managed to do either. It was only later that I understood what Bea was doing. Every exercise was designed so that we could not fail at it. By the time she asked us to let go of the side, we had stopped expecting to.
cards.question: What does the writer come to understand about Bea's method?
choices: It was intended to save time later in the course.
It was not really suitable for complete beginners.
It was more about breathing than about swimming.
It slowly removed the learners' expectation of failure.
cards.highlight: By the time she asked us to let go of the side, we had stopped expecting to.
cards.why: Every exercise was one 'we could not fail at', so by the end they 'had stopped expecting to' fail. C repeats her early complaint, which she later sees was mistaken.

cards.text: Leonard was the first of us to swim a full width of the pool. He did it in late October, slowly and with his head held very high, like a man trying to keep a hat dry. When he reached the far side, the rest of us cheered so loudly that a lifeguard came over to see what had happened. Leonard pretended to be embarrassed by the fuss, but he talked about nothing else for the rest of the evening. I remember feeling delighted for him and, at the same time, slightly jealous, which I would not have admitted then.
cards.question: How did the writer feel when Leonard swam a width of the pool?
choices: Worried that he might hurt himself.
Happy for him, but also wishing it had been her.
Embarrassed by the noise the group made.
Amused by the way he looked in the water.
cards.highlight: I remember feeling delighted for him and, at the same time, slightly jealous
cards.why: 'Delighted for him and, at the same time, slightly jealous.' The hat comparison is the writer's humour now, not how she felt then; it was Leonard who pretended to be embarrassed.

cards.text: My own progress was less straightforward. In December I caught a heavy cold and missed three lessons, and when I came back it was as if I had forgotten everything. I stood at the edge, unable to make myself get in, while the others swam past. Bea did not try to persuade me. She just handed me a float and said I could hold it for as long as I liked. I held it for the whole of that lesson, and most of the next. Afterwards she told me that going backwards was part of the process, and that almost everyone did it at some point.
cards.question: What point does the writer make about Bea in this paragraph?
choices: She was disappointed that the writer had missed lessons.
She made the writer practise on her own.
She accepted the writer's setback without putting pressure on her.
She expected the writer to give up the course.
cards.highlight: Bea did not try to persuade me.
cards.why: She 'did not try to persuade' her and let her hold the float 'for as long as I liked', then called going backwards 'part of the process'. Nothing shows disappointment.

cards.text: I swam my first length in March: twenty-five metres of untidy breaststroke, which took me nearly two minutes. Nobody cheered, because by then lengths were nothing special in our group, and I found that I did not mind at all. I still swim twice a week, usually early, when the pool is almost empty. I am not fast, and I doubt I ever will be. But last summer, on a beach in Cornwall, my nephew asked who would look after the bags, and for the first time in my life I told him somebody else would have to.
cards.question: What is the writer's main point in the final paragraph?
choices: Learning to swim has changed how she behaves in a situation she used to avoid.
She is disappointed that she has not become a faster swimmer.
She was hurt that nobody celebrated her first length.
She now prefers swimming alone to swimming with others.
cards.highlight: for the first time in my life I told him somebody else would have to
cards.why: The bags take us back to the first paragraph: she no longer needs an excuse to stay out of the water. She 'did not mind' the silence and simply accepts she is not fast.
